parsed.hook: Sonoma Mountain’s volcanic loam doesn’t just drain fast—it forces Chardonnay roots to dig deep, pulling up minerals that taste like wet granite and crushed oyster shell. Paul Hobbs’ Richard Dinner Cuvee Agustina sits at 1,200 feet, above the fog line, where cool Pacific air collides with afternoon sun, keeping acidity razor-sharp even as the grapes ripen fully.
parsed.wine_summary: This is not the buttery, oak-bomb Chardonnay that defined California in the 1990s. Hobbs farms the Agustina block on Sonoma Mountain’s eastern slope, where 40-year-old vines grow in rocky volcanic loam over fractured basalt. The site’s elevation—above the morning fog—extends hang time, letting grapes develop phenolic ripeness without losing acidity. Hobbs’ winemaking leans into restraint: native yeast fermentation in French oak (30% new), full malolactic conversion, and 11 months of lees aging without bâtonnage. The result is a Chardonnay that splits the difference between Côte de Beaune richness and Sonoma Coast tension, with a saline edge that comes from the site’s proximity to the San Pablo Bay’s marine layer.
parsed.terroir_expression: Sonoma Mountain’s volcanic soils—derived from the Sonoma Volcanics formation—are a mix of rhyolitic tuff and clay loam, with chunks of basalt that retain heat during the day and release it at night. The AVA’s elevation (400–2,295 feet) creates a diurnal swing of up to 40°F, preserving acidity while allowing slow, even ripening. The Agustina block’s specific location on the eastern slope means it catches the first morning sun but avoids the harsh afternoon heat that hits the western side. This combination of soil, elevation, and exposure produces Chardonnay with a distinct mineral streak—think crushed rock and saline—alongside ripe stone fruit and a textural grip that’s rare in California.
parsed.vinification_summary: Hobbs picks early for Chardonnay, often at 23–24° Brix, to retain acidity. The fruit is whole-cluster pressed, then fermented in French oak barrels (30% new) using native yeasts. Full malolactic fermentation softens the acidity but doesn’t erase it, thanks to the wine’s natural tension. Hobbs skips bâtonnage (lees stirring), letting the lees settle naturally to avoid over-extracting creaminess. The wine ages for 11 months in barrel before bottling without fining or filtration. The lack of bâtonnage is key: it preserves the wine’s linear structure and mineral focus, preventing the cloying richness that can come from overworked lees.

parsed.value_assessment: $85–$110. At this price, it competes with Kistler’s Sonoma Mountain Chardonnay ($120) and Peter Michael’s ‘Belle Côte’ ($100). It’s worth the premium over generic Sonoma Coast Chardonnays because of the site’s specificity—you’re paying for volcanic soil and elevation, not just the Hobbs name. parsed.market_position: This wine lives on high-end retail shelves and sommelier lists in restaurants that prioritize site-driven California Chardonnay. It’s a favorite among collectors who chase volcanic soil influence (think Etna Bianco or Santorini) but want a New World expression. Casual drinkers often find it too austere—it’s not the kind of Chardonnay you’d pair with popcorn or buttered lobster rolls.
parsed.insider_take: Most people assume this is just another expensive California Chardonnay, but the Agustina block’s volcanic soils make it one of the few that can stand up to white Burgundy in blind tastings. The tradeoff? It’s not as immediately charming as a buttery, oak-forward Napa Chardonnay—you have to meet it halfway, pairing it with food that highlights its acidity and minerality. If you prefer your whites soft and fruity, skip it. If you want a Chardonnay that tastes like a place, not a winemaking recipe, this is it.
